vignette:
Dr. Marcus Thorne still prides himself on the steadiness of his hands. For thirty-five years, that steadiness has been the bedrock of his identity, the source of his craft as a dentist. Now, at fifty-eight, he finds himself pausing before picking up a periodontal probe, taking a deep, quiet breath to quell a tremor no one else can see. The bright, circular operating light above the patient’s chair is often the problem. It can catch his eye at the wrong angle and, for a disorienting second, it’s no longer a tool for illumination but the blinding white of headlights pinning him in place.

It’s been nine months since the incident. He was driving home from a late study club meeting, a route he’d taken thousands of times. He remembers the sudden flash of blue and red lights filling his rearview mirror. He pulled over immediately, his mind cycling through benign possibilities—a broken taillight, perhaps? He had his license and registration on the passenger seat before the officer even reached his window. The beam of a flashlight scanned his face, his hands, the backseat. The questions were sharp, accusatory. He was asked to step out of the car. Marcus, a man who commands respect in his community and his practice, complied with the quiet dignity he’d always possessed.

He can’t recall the exact sequence of what happened next, only a cascade of sensations. The officer’s voice escalating, the sudden shove from behind that sent him stumbling forward, the rough scrape of asphalt against his cheek and the side of his face. He remembers the cold, tight bite of handcuffs and the bewildering shame of being searched on the side of the road, the officer’s knee pressing into his back. It was a case of mistaken identity, they later said. A car matching his model was involved in a robbery. He was released within an hour, with a gruff, dismissive apology.

He drove home that night in a silent fog and told his partner, Sarah, that he was fine, just tired. For a few weeks, he believed it. But the world had tilted on its axis. The predictable order he had built his life around felt like a fragile illusion. Sleep became a battlefield. He’d jolt awake, heart hammering against his ribs, the phantom feeling of gravel on his skin. He started taking the long way home from his office to avoid the stretch of road where it happened. When Sarah suggests a nighttime drive to look at city lights, a knot of ice forms in his stomach and he makes an excuse about his eyes being tired.

At work, his sanctuary of sterile precision has become a landscape of potential threats. The waiting room, once a peaceful space, now feels fraught with unseen tension. He finds himself mentally cataloging the posture of every person waiting, bracing for a sudden movement. The sharp, unexpected clang of a dropped instrument makes him flinch violently, a jolt of pure adrenaline that leaves him shaky and unnerved. His assistant has learned to move around him with a quiet, deliberate slowness.

He feels a profound sense of detachment. When he’s with Sarah, he feels as if he’s watching their life through a thick pane of glass. She’ll touch his arm and he won’t register it for a moment. He knows she’s worried; he sees the concern in her eyes when he stares blankly at the television, the news reports of police encounters sending a cold dread through him until he has to get up and leave the room. He has stopped trying to explain the persistent, simmering anger that lives in his chest, an anger at his own powerlessness. The work that once brought him satisfaction now feels like a series of mechanical movements. He looks at his own steady hands, the hands of a healer and a craftsman, and remembers them cuffed behind his back, useless.
